newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Second Earth Summit opens with warning of disaster.
newsitem.headline: Second Earth Summit opens with warning of disaster.

text.p: The second Earth Summit opened on Monday with a stark warning that the planet might soon pass "the point of no return" if environmental plunder and pollution did not stop.

With more than 60 prime ministers and presidents slated to speak in a marathon week-long summit of 173 countries, a confrontation immediately emerged between rich and poor nations and between Europe and the United States
The Third World wants financing to help the Third World develop without ravaging the earth.
"The general trend for the whole world, whether we consider countries or individuals, has been for the rich to become richer and the poor to become poorer," Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe said.
Meanwhile, European states pressed on with an attack they launched on the United States at last weekend's Group of Seven summit in Denver.
They say the world's wealthiest nation is its chief polluter and attack its reluctance to set specific targets on cutting global warming.
U.N. General Assembly President Razali Ismail of Malaysia began the session with a plea to political leaders "to come to the rescue."
"We as a species, as a planet, are teetering on the edge, living unsustainably and perpetuating inequity, and may soon pass the point of no return," he warned.
This week's conference comes five years after a heady summit in Rio de Janeiro where 10,000 diplomats and environmentalists outlined an ambitious blueprint to safeguard the planet.
But speakers after speaker here expressed dismay that action since Rio fell far short of what was needed.
"Our task for the coming days mut be to chart the course for the years to come, "Vice President Al Gore said in a welcoming speech. President Bill Clinton is to address the conference on Thursday.

"Today greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise at record rates. Unless we change course, during the lives of our grandchildren the concentration of these gases in the atmosphere will reach levels not seen on this planet for more than 50 million years," Gore said.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, on his first visit to the United Nations during his 15 years in office, proposed a "global umbrella organisation" for environmental issues, with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) "as a major pillar." He gave few details.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair launched a thinly veiled attack on the United States and Canada in his first speech to the United Nations.
"I attacked the last British government for many things. But they did deliver on the greenhouse gas emission targets set in Rio," he said.

"Some other countries cannot say the same, including some of the great industrialised nations," he added. "To them I say this: our targets will not be taken seriously by the poorer countries until the richer countries are meeting them."

Many envoys hoped that the United States would come up with goals to reduce greenhouse gas emissions responsible for climate change. But President Clinton pointedly rejected European pressure to set specific targets during the Denver summit.
The European Union has called for a 15 percent reduction of greenhouse gases by 2010.

The United States accounts for nearly 23 percent of all greenhouse gases produced when fossil fuels like oil and coal are burned. Scientists say these emissions will lead to dangerous climate changes in the next century.
Most rich countries agreed in principle in Rio to increase foreign aid to 0.7 percent of their gross national product. But since then aid has declined from 0.35 percent to 0.27 percent in 1995.
Only the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Sweden topped the 0.7 percent goal. Once the world's biggest donor, the United States is now in fifth place.
